q: Which of these is the best definition of **decomposition**?
options: Removing unnecessary detail from a problem
Breaking a problem down into smaller sub-problems
Converting an algorithm into program code
Testing an algorithm with a trace table
ms: B — decomposition breaks a complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems.

q: Which of these is the best definition of **abstraction**?
options: Writing an algorithm as a flowchart
Removing unnecessary detail to focus on what matters
Repeating instructions until a condition is met
ms: C — abstraction removes/hides detail that is not needed to solve the problem.

q: A developer splits a game into separate parts: player movement, scoring, sound and graphics. This is an example of
ms: C — the problem has been broken into sub-problems: decomposition.

q: A satnav map shows roads and junctions but not trees or the colour of buildings. This is an example of
ms: B — irrelevant real-world detail has been removed: abstraction.

q: An algorithm must ask for exactly **12** monthly rainfall values. The most appropriate construct is a
ms: A — the number of repetitions (12) is known in advance, so a count-controlled FOR loop fits best.

q: An algorithm must keep asking for a password until the correct one is entered. The input must be requested **at least once**. The most appropriate loop is
ms: C — REPEAT…UNTIL runs the body first then checks, guaranteeing at least one attempt.

q: A WHILE loop differs from a REPEAT…UNTIL loop because a WHILE loop
options: checks its condition before the body runs
ms: B — WHILE is pre-condition: if the condition is false at the start, the body never runs.

q: Which construct should be used to give a 10% discount **only** when `total > 50`?
ms: B — a choice based on a condition is selection (IF).

q: In a flowchart, a loop is created when
options: a flowline returns to an earlier point in the chart
a process box contains a calculation
an input and output appear in the same chart
ms: B — iteration in a flowchart is shown by a flowline going back to an earlier symbol, controlled by a decision.

q: Every exit line from a decision symbol must be
ms: B — decision exits must be labelled so the reader knows which branch is followed.

q: Which symbol should hold the step **SEND "Well done" TO DISPLAY** in a flowchart?
ms: C — displaying a message is output, drawn as a parallelogram.

q: Which symbol should hold the step **SET count TO count + 1** in a flowchart?
ms: B — a calculation/assignment is a process: rectangle.

q: Which line correctly asks the user for a value in Edexcel pseudocode?
ms: C — Edexcel pseudocode uses RECEIVE <variable> FROM KEYBOARD.

q: Which line correctly initialises a running total?
ms: A — the total must be set to 0 before the loop starts adding to it.

q: `85 DIV 10` evaluates to
ms: B — DIV is whole-number division: 85 ÷ 10 = 8 remainder 5, so 8.

q: `85 MOD 10` evaluates to
ms: C — MOD gives the remainder: 85 = 8×10 + **5**.

q: To convert 200 minutes into whole hours, an algorithm should use
ms: B — DIV 60 gives the whole hours (3); MOD 60 would give the leftover minutes (20).

q: A number `n` is even when
ms: B — even numbers leave remainder 0 when divided by 2.

q:
Which condition keeps a validation loop repeating **until** an age between 11 and 18 inclusive is entered?

`REPEAT … UNTIL ______`
ms: C — the loop stops when the input is valid: at least 11 AND at most 18. Option A wrongly excludes 11 and 18.

q: In a max-finding algorithm, `max` is best initialised to
options: the first value in the list
the last value in the list
ms: B — starting with the first value works for all data. Initialising to 0 fails when every value is negative.

q: A **sentinel** (rogue) value is used to
options: validate that input is in range
signal the end of a stream of inputs
count how many times a loop runs
ms: B — a rogue value such as -1 tells the loop to stop reading further input.

q: Which loop header processes inputs **until** the rogue value -1 is entered, checking before each iteration?
ms: B — WHILE num <> -1 keeps looping while the value is not the sentinel.

q: An algorithm is **fit for purpose** when it
options: produces the correct output for every valid input
ms: B — fitness for purpose means it correctly solves the problem it was designed for.

q: Two correct algorithms solve the same problem. Algorithm A makes 100 comparisons; Algorithm B makes 20. Algorithm B is
ms: B — same result with fewer steps/comparisons = more efficient.

q: A search loop keeps running through the whole list even after finding the target. The best efficiency improvement is to
options: exit the loop as soon as the target is found
ms: B — stopping early avoids unnecessary comparisons.

q: Which is a benefit of decomposition when a **team** builds software?
options: Sub-problems can be shared between team members
ms: B — separate sub-problems can be worked on in parallel by different people.

q: When creating a computer card game, which detail would abstraction most likely **remove**?
options: The pattern printed on the back of the cards
The number of cards in the deck
ms: C — the back design does not affect gameplay; value, suit and deck size do.

q: The three basic programming constructs are
ms: B — sequence (in order), selection (choice), iteration (repetition).

q: `FOR i FROM 10 TO 2 STEP -2 DO` — how many times does the loop body run?
ms: B — i takes 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 → five iterations.

q: Which line correctly swaps the contents of `a` and `b` after `SET temp TO a`?
options: SET a TO temp, SET b TO a
SET a TO b, SET b TO temp
SET b TO a, SET a TO b
SET temp TO b, SET a TO temp
ms: B — with a saved in temp: a takes b's value, then b takes temp (a's original value).

q: The first stage in creating an algorithm should be to
options: understand the problem and identify inputs and outputs
ms: B — you must understand the problem and its inputs/outputs before designing a solution.

q: Which of these tasks is best solved with **selection but no iteration**?
options: Deciding whether a single year is a leap year
ms: B — one decision about one value needs IF only; the others all repeat, so need loops.

q: A flowchart has a decision "count < 10?" whose **Yes** branch leads back up to a process "count = count + 1". This section of the chart is
ms: C — the backwards flowline controlled by a counting condition forms a count-controlled loop.

q: Describe what is meant by **decomposition**. (2)
ms: Breaking a problem down (1) into smaller sub-problems that can each be solved separately (1).

q: Describe what is meant by **abstraction**. (2)
ms: Removing/hiding unnecessary detail (1) so that only the information needed to solve the problem is considered (1).

q: State **two** benefits of decomposing a large problem before writing an algorithm. (2)
ms: Any two: smaller parts are easier to solve/understand (1); parts can be shared between people (1); parts can be tested individually (1); parts can be reused in other programs (1).

q: Describe how abstraction could be applied to playing cards when creating a card game to run on a computer. (2)
ms: Keep only the details that matter to the game, e.g. suit and value of each card (1); ignore/remove details such as the design on the back, texture or exact artwork (1).

q: A developer is creating a satnav app. Describe how abstraction is used in the map it displays. (2)
ms: Only relevant detail is included, e.g. roads, junctions, distances (1); unnecessary real-world detail such as building appearance, trees or colours is removed (1).

q: Explain why a running total variable must be initialised **before** a loop starts. (2)
ms: So it starts from a known value of 0 (1); otherwise it holds an unknown/previous value, or is reset every iteration if set inside the loop, giving a wrong total (1).

q: Explain **one** difference between a WHILE loop and a REPEAT…UNTIL loop. (2)
ms: WHILE tests its condition before the body, so it may run zero times (1); REPEAT…UNTIL tests after the body, so it always runs at least once (1). (Also creditworthy: WHILE repeats while true; REPEAT stops when true.)

q: Explain why a FOR loop is more appropriate than a WHILE loop for processing the marks of exactly 30 students. (2)
ms: The number of repetitions is known in advance / fixed at 30 (1); a FOR loop counts automatically so no separate counter variable and condition need managing (1).

q: State the purpose of a **sentinel (rogue) value** and give an example. (2)
ms: A special input that signals no more data / stops the input loop (1); e.g. entering -1 (or 0, "STOP") to end entry of exam marks (1).

q: An algorithm asks for a percentage. Explain why the input should be **validated**. (2)
ms: To reject impossible values (e.g. below 0 or above 100) (1) so the algorithm only processes sensible data / does not produce incorrect results or crash (1).

q: State **two** rules that must be followed when drawing a flowchart. (2)
ms: Any two: exactly one Start (1); flowlines have arrows showing direction (1); decision symbols have two labelled exits (Yes/No) (1); every route ends at an End/terminator (1); correct symbol shapes used for each step type (1).

q: Explain why the exits of a decision symbol must be labelled. (2)
ms: So the reader knows which branch is followed when the condition is true and which when it is false (1); without labels the flowchart is ambiguous / could be followed incorrectly (1).

q: Describe what is meant by an algorithm being **fit for purpose**. (2)
ms: It solves the problem it was designed to solve (1), producing the correct output for every valid input (1).

q: Two correct algorithms find a name in a list. Explain what would make one of them more **efficient** than the other. (2)
ms: It completes the task in fewer steps/comparisons (1), e.g. stopping the search as soon as the name is found instead of checking the rest of the list (1).

q:
State the construct (sequence, selection or iteration) used in each case:

(a) checking whether a customer is old enough to buy a ticket
(b) adding VAT to a price then displaying it (2)
ms: (a) selection (1) — a decision based on a condition. (b) sequence (1) — steps carried out in order, one after another.

q:
State the construct (sequence, selection or iteration) used in each case:

(a) asking for a PIN again and again until it is correct
(b) choosing between three postage prices based on parcel weight (2)
ms: (a) iteration (1) — the request repeats. (b) selection (1) — one option is chosen using conditions (IF/ELSE IF/ELSE).

q:
A program will calculate the total cost of items scanned at a till, stopping when a barcode of 0 is scanned.

Identify **one** input, **one** process and **one** output of this algorithm. (3)
ms: Input: the price/barcode of each item scanned (1). Process: adding each price to a running total (accept: checking for the 0 sentinel) (1). Output: the total cost displayed (1).

q:
Complete the sentence.

Breaking a problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve is called ______. (1)
ms: decomposition (1).

q:
Complete the sentence.

Removing unnecessary detail from a problem so only the important information remains is called ______. (1)
ms: abstraction (1).

q:
Complete the sentence.

A loop that runs a fixed number of times, counting automatically, is a ______ loop. (1)
ms: FOR (count-controlled) loop (1).

q:
Complete the sentence.

A ______ value, such as -1, is entered to tell an input loop that there is no more data. (1)
ms: sentinel / rogue (1).

q:
Complete the sentence.

In Edexcel pseudocode, results are displayed using SEND … TO ______. (1)
ms: DISPLAY (1).

q:
Complete the sentences.

A REPEAT…UNTIL loop checks its condition ______ the loop body runs, so the body always runs at least ______ time(s). (2)
ms: after (1); one (1).

q:
Complete the sentences.

In a flowchart, a calculation is written in a ______ symbol, while a question with Yes/No exits is written in a ______ symbol. (2)
ms: process / rectangle (1); decision / diamond (1).

q:
Match each task to the most appropriate construct (sequence, selection, iteration).

**1** Display a menu, then ask for a choice
**2** Repeat a question until a valid answer is given
**3** Award a bonus only if the score is over 100 (3)
ms: 1 → sequence (1); 2 → iteration (1); 3 → selection (1).

q:
Match each task to the most appropriate loop (FOR, WHILE, REPEAT…UNTIL).

**1** Print the 7 times table from 1×7 to 12×7
**2** Keep asking for a password until it is correct
**3** Process customer orders while there are orders in the queue (possibly none) (3)
ms: 1 → FOR (count known) (1); 2 → REPEAT…UNTIL (must run at least once) (1); 3 → WHILE (may run zero times) (1).

q:
Match each description to **decomposition**, **abstraction** or **algorithm**.

**1** A step-by-step set of instructions to solve a problem
**2** Splitting a quiz app into: question display, answer checking, score keeping
**3** Storing a student as just a name and a mark, ignoring hair colour and height (3)
ms: 1 → algorithm (1); 2 → decomposition (1); 3 → abstraction (1).

q:
A weather app shows temperature and rain chance for each hour.

State **one** piece of information the app's designers kept and **one** they abstracted away from the real weather. (2)
ms: Kept: temperature / rain probability / wind for each hour (1). Removed: any real-world detail not needed, e.g. exact cloud shapes, individual raindrops, humidity at every altitude (1).

q: A developer is building a chess program. State **two** details of a real chess set that abstraction would remove. (2)
ms: Any two irrelevant physical details: colour/material of the pieces (1); carving style/appearance (1); weight/size of pieces or board texture (1). (Position, piece type and legal moves must be kept.)

q: A school is building a system to run its sports day. Decompose the problem into **three** sensible sub-problems. (3)
ms: Any three distinct sub-problems, e.g.: recording entries for each event (1); timing/recording results (1); calculating team points (1); producing/printing the leaderboard (1); scheduling events (1).

q: A developer is creating an online shop. Decompose the shop into **three** sub-problems. (3)
ms: Any three, e.g.: product catalogue/search (1); shopping basket (1); payment processing (1); user accounts/login (1); order tracking/delivery (1).

q: Explain **one** reason why decomposed sub-problems are easier to **test** than a whole program. (2)
ms: Each sub-problem can be tested separately/in isolation (1), so errors are found and located more easily because only a small amount of code is involved (1).

q: Explain why a programmer might **reuse** a solution to a sub-problem in another program. (2)
ms: The sub-problem (e.g. validating a date) also occurs in other programs (1); reusing tested code saves time and reduces errors (1).

q:
An algorithm uses `RECEIVE mark FROM KEYBOARD` inside a FOR loop that runs 30 times.

Explain why the line `SET total TO 0` must appear **before** the loop rather than inside it. (2)
ms: Inside the loop it would reset the total to 0 on every iteration (1), so the final total would only equal the last mark instead of the sum of all 30 (1).

q:
A validation loop accepts test scores from 0 to 50 inclusive.

Write the condition that should complete: `REPEAT … UNTIL ______`. (2)
ms: (score >= 0) AND (score <= 50) (2) — one mark for both comparisons correct with >=/<=, one for AND joining them.

q: A programmer writes `WHILE (choice <> 1) OR (choice <> 2) DO` to re-ask for a menu choice of 1 or 2. Explain why this loop never ends. (2)
ms: Any value fails at least one of the two inequalities, so the OR condition is always true (1); the operator should be AND: WHILE (choice <> 1) AND (choice <> 2) (1).

q: Explain why an algorithm that never sends anything to the display would fail a fitness-for-purpose check, even if its calculations are correct. (2)
ms: The user never receives the result / there is no output (1), so the algorithm does not achieve its purpose of communicating the answer (1).

q: State what is meant by a **count-controlled** loop and a **condition-controlled** loop. (2)
ms: Count-controlled: repeats a fixed number of times, e.g. FOR (1). Condition-controlled: repeats depending on a condition, so the number of repetitions is not known in advance, e.g. WHILE or REPEAT…UNTIL (1).

q: A cinema charges: child £5, adult £9. State the selection statement structure needed and why a loop is **not** needed to price a single ticket. (2)
ms: An IF…THEN…ELSE choosing between the two prices based on age/type (1); nothing repeats for one ticket, so no iteration is required (1).

q:
An algorithm reads prices until -1 is entered, then displays the number of prices and their average.

Identify **three** variables the algorithm needs and state the purpose of each. (3)
ms: price — holds each input (1); total — running sum of prices (1); count — how many prices were entered (used with total to compute the average) (1).

q: Give **two** reasons why sensible variable names (e.g. `total` rather than `t`) help when creating algorithms. (2)
ms: Any two: the purpose of each variable is clear, making the algorithm easier to understand/follow (1); errors are easier to spot (1); easier for others (or an examiner) to read and maintain (1).

q:
A flowchart for a quiz must add 1 to `score` when an answer is correct, and do nothing extra otherwise.

State the symbol used for the check and the symbol used for adding to the score. (2)
ms: Check: decision (diamond) (1). Adding to score: process (rectangle) (1).

q:
A gym charges by age: under 16 → £3, 16 to 64 → £6, 65 and over → £4.

Explain why IF … ELSE IF … ELSE is more appropriate here than three separate IF statements. (3)
ms: The categories are mutually exclusive — only one price can apply (1); ELSE IF stops checking once a condition matches, so it is more efficient (1); separate IFs risk overlapping conditions being written wrongly / all being tested unnecessarily (1).

q:
An algorithm calculates change as a number of pence, e.g. 178.

Explain how DIV and MOD can be used to express this as pounds and pence. (2)
ms: 178 DIV 100 gives the pounds (1) (1 here); 178 MOD 100 gives the remaining pence (78) (1).

q: State the output of `SEND 47 DIV 5 TO DISPLAY` and `SEND 47 MOD 5 TO DISPLAY`. (2)

A student writes an algorithm and wants to check it is fit for purpose before coding it.

Describe how a **trace table** helps with this. (3)
ms: The algorithm is dry-run by hand line by line (1); the value of each variable (and any output) is recorded at each step (1); the recorded outputs are compared with the expected results to confirm correctness / locate logic errors (1).

q: State **two** types of test data that should be used to check an algorithm that accepts exam marks from 0 to 100. (2)
ms: Any two: normal data (e.g. 57) (1); boundary data (0, 100) (1); erroneous/invalid data (e.g. -5, 101, "ten") (1).

q:
An algorithm re-calculates `numberOfItems * VAT_RATE` inside a loop that runs 1,000 times, even though the result never changes.

State the efficiency improvement and why it works. (2)
ms: Calculate it once before the loop and store it in a variable (1); this avoids repeating the same calculation 1,000 times, reducing the number of steps (1).

q:
A linear search algorithm continues to the end of the list even after finding the target value.

State the improvement and its effect. (2)
ms: Exit/stop the loop as soon as the target is found (1); on average far fewer comparisons are made, so the search is more efficient (1).

q: Explain why an algorithm should be designed and traced **before** it is coded in a programming language. (2)
ms: Design errors/logic errors are found early when they are cheap and easy to fix (1); the design acts as a plan, so coding is faster and less error-prone (also creditworthy: design is language-independent) (1).

q: State **one** advantage of designing an algorithm as a flowchart and **one** advantage of designing it in pseudocode. (2)
ms: Flowchart: visual — the flow, decisions and loops are easy to see at a glance (1). Pseudocode: closer to real code, so quicker to write for long algorithms and easier to convert to a program (1).

q:
A student draws a flowchart where one branch of a decision never reaches an End symbol.

Explain the problem this causes. (2)
ms: That route through the algorithm never terminates / the reader cannot tell what happens next (1); the flowchart is incomplete/invalid, and if implemented could leave the program running or undefined (1).

q:
A ticket machine algorithm must: receive the number of tickets, calculate cost at £4.50 each, add a £1 booking fee, and display the total.

Write down the **order** of the four steps and name the construct that orders them. (3)
ms: Receive number → calculate tickets × 4.50 → add 1 booking fee → display total (2 for correct sensible order; 1 if one step misplaced). Construct: sequence (1).

q:
A game awards: 3 points for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss, and doubles the points if it was a cup match.

State the constructs needed and the order in which the two decisions should be made. (3)
ms: Selection to choose 3/1/0 based on result (1); a second selection to double if cup match (1); the result points must be decided first, then doubled — doubling before deciding would use the wrong value (1).

q: Explain why the condition `WHILE count < 10` combined with forgetting `SET count TO count + 1` inside the loop produces an infinite loop. (2)
ms: count never changes, so it stays below 10 (1); the condition therefore remains true forever and the loop never exits (1).

q: A REPEAT…UNTIL validation loop is preferred over WHILE for asking a user for input. Explain why. (2)
ms: The input must be requested at least once before it can be checked (1); REPEAT…UNTIL runs the body first, which matches this naturally, whereas WHILE would need the input reading twice or a fake initial value (1).

q:
A robot vacuum's algorithm is decomposed into: mapping the room, planning a route, avoiding obstacles, returning to charge.

Explain **one** way abstraction would also be used in the mapping sub-problem. (3)
ms: The map keeps only the details needed for cleaning (1), e.g. positions of walls/furniture as obstacles (1), ignoring irrelevant detail such as colours, patterns on the carpet or objects on shelves (1).

q:
State whether each is decomposition or abstraction:

(a) A London Underground map showing stations as dots and lines, not real distances
(b) Splitting 'make a weather app' into: fetch data, store data, display forecast (2)
ms: (a) abstraction (1) — unnecessary geographic detail removed. (b) decomposition (1) — the problem is split into sub-problems.

q:
An algorithm finds the smallest of 20 entered numbers.

State the initialisation used for `min`, the comparison made inside the loop, and the update performed when the comparison is true. (3)
ms: Initialise min to the first number entered (1); compare each new number: IF num < min (1); update: SET min TO num (1).

q:
A student's algorithm works for normal data but crashes when the very first input is the sentinel -1 (dividing by zero when averaging).

State the check that should be added and where. (2)
ms: Before dividing, check IF count > 0 (or count <> 0) (1); only calculate/display the average inside that check, otherwise display a suitable message (1).

q: Describe the **three** steps a programmer should take between being given a problem and starting to write pseudocode. (3)
ms: Understand the problem / identify the expected outcome (1); identify the inputs, processes and outputs (1); decompose the problem into smaller sub-problems (accept: choose suitable constructs/plan the logic) (1).

q:
A parking machine takes payment in whole pounds, 1 to 24, and prints a ticket showing the exit time.

Give one example each of **normal**, **boundary** and **erroneous** test data for the payment input. (3)
ms: Normal: e.g. 5 (1). Boundary: 1 or 24 (1). Erroneous: e.g. 0, 25, -3 or "two" (1).

q:
A developer is creating a football management game. Players are stored with a name, position and skill rating. The game is split into teams, transfers, match simulation and finances.

Discuss the use of **decomposition and abstraction** in developing this game. (6)
ms: Level-marked. Decomposition: the game is broken into sub-problems (teams, transfers, match simulation, finances); each is smaller and easier to design, code and test; work can be divided among developers; modules like finances could be reused. Abstraction: real footballers are reduced to name, position and skill rating; irrelevant details (appearance, personal life, exact running style) are removed; the match simulation models only what affects results. Strong answers link both terms to THIS game with examples and explain the benefits (easier development, testing, manageable data). 5–6: both concepts, applied, with benefits; 3–4: both defined with some application; 1–2: definitions only.

q:
A student must design an algorithm for a school library fine calculator before coding it. She can design it as a flowchart or in pseudocode.

Discuss the choice between flowchart and pseudocode for designing this algorithm. (6)
ms: Level-marked. Flowchart: visual; decisions (e.g. is the book late? over 30 days?) and loops are easy to follow; good for communicating with non-programmers; but becomes large/unwieldy for long algorithms and is slow to redraw when changed. Pseudocode: quicker to write and edit; closer to final code so easier to translate; handles long/complex logic compactly; but less visual and needs consistent keywords. Both are language-independent design tools; either can be traced. A justified conclusion (e.g. flowchart for the simple fine decision structure, pseudocode if it grows) gains the top level. 5–6: balanced, applied, justified conclusion; 3–4: some advantages/disadvantages of both; 1–2: generic points on one.

q: Explain why an algorithm's **efficiency** matters more when it processes a very large data set than a small one. (3)
ms: Extra/unnecessary steps are repeated for every data item (1); with millions of items, small inefficiencies multiply into significant time (or resource) costs (1); with a small data set both versions finish quickly, so the difference is barely noticeable (1).

q:
A colleague suggests testing an algorithm only with normal data 'because that's what users will type'.

Explain why this is not enough to show the algorithm is fit for purpose. (2)
ms: Errors often occur at boundaries or with invalid input (1); the algorithm must handle every valid input correctly and reject erroneous input sensibly, so boundary and erroneous data must also be tested (1).

q:
A smart doorbell is being developed. It should detect a visitor, record a short video, send an alert to the owner's phone and let the owner speak to the visitor.

(a) Decompose the doorbell system into **two** sensible sub-problems. (2)
(b) Describe **one** use of abstraction when storing information about each visit. (2)
ms: (a) Any two of: motion/visitor detection (1); video recording/storage (1); sending phone alerts (1); two-way audio (1). (b) Store only relevant data such as time/date and the video clip (1), ignoring unnecessary detail such as weather, passers-by or the visitor's clothing colours (1).
